body: EU AI Act Article 25 is the sleeper provision that rewires AI procurement. It states that any distributor, importer, deployer, or third party that (a) puts its name or trademark on a high-risk AI system already placed on the market, (b) makes a substantial modification to a high-risk AI system, or (c) modifies the intended purpose of an AI system such that it becomes high-risk -- shall be considered a provider and shall assume all provider obligations under the Act. This is not a footnote: it means a hospital that fine-tunes a general-purpose model for clinical triage becomes the provider for regulatory purposes. A government agency that repurposes a commercial NLP system for citizen-benefit eligibility screening inherits Article 9 risk management and Article 17 quality management duties. The Council of AI treats Article 25 as a boundary-attribution rule: the entity closest to the modification is the one whose signature must travel with the artifact. For a verification-first operator, this means every substantial modification must create a new verified measurement credential chained to the upstream credential, forming a tamper-evident provenance chain. The posture is monitored containment, not provable isolation -- the chain proves who modified what and when, not that the modification was safe. The key shift for procurement teams: the buy-dont-build strategy does not dodge provider obligations if you substantially modify what you bought.
context: 2026-09-01 engine cycle -- EU AI Act Article 25 now binding (Aug 2, 2026); the value-chain cascade rule: when a distributor, importer, or deployer modifies a high-risk AI system, they become the provider and inherit full obligations.
